summary: RFC 4762 describes withdrawing learned MAC addresses in a VPLS for faster convergence after topology changes. This document defines an enhanced withdraw procedure with an empty MAC list for hierarchical VPLS, to avoid unneeded relearning.

eli5.summary: When a road closes, a delivery company should forget only routes that no longer work. This RFC helps virtual LAN switches forget fewer addresses so they relearn less.

subtitle: A targeted MAC flush for hierarchical VPLS, so a failover clears only the addresses that went stale.

tldr.problem: When a dual-homed H-VPLS fails over to a backup pseudowire, the existing empty-list MAC withdraw makes every PE flush addresses that were not affected, causing needless flooding and relearning.
tldr.mechanism: A new MAC Flush Parameters TLV (0x0406) with an N flag set to 1 tells receivers to flush only the MAC addresses learned from the sender ("flush-all-from-me"), and sub-TLVs scope the flush by B-MAC and I-SID in PBB-VPLS.
tldr.outcome: Only the stale addresses are relearned, which cuts disruption and black-holing time. All devices must understand the TLV, since there is no negotiation.

today: RFC 7361 is a Proposed Standard (September 2014), and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It augments the MAC withdraw procedures of RFC 4762 rather than replacing them.

sections.title: H-VPLS and MAC Withdrawal
sections.content:
A Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS), described in RFC 4762, is built from point-to-point pseudowires (PWs) in a flat full mesh between Provider Edge (PE) devices. These devices learn and forward on Ethernet MAC addresses. Adding non-meshed spoke nodes gives a Hierarchical VPLS (H-VPLS). RFC 7041 adds Provider Backbone Bridging (PBB) to VPLS, called PBB-VPLS.

RFC 4762 defines a MAC address withdrawal so that learned MAC addresses are removed for faster convergence after topology changes. A typical case is a dual-homed edge device, the MTU-s, connected to two PEs by a primary and a backup spoke PW. RFC 7361 says it aims to clarify several dual-homing models used in practice and the uses of LDP-based MAC flushing in them.

The document uses the term MAC flush message for an LDP address withdraw message with an empty MAC list. Its solutions apply only to those messages.
sections.eli5: A big virtual network learns which address lives behind which door. When a door closes, the network has to unlearn the addresses that used it.

sections.title: The Problem with Flushing Everything
sections.content:
In the dual-homed example, the MAC addresses behind the customer sites are learned by the other PEs over their mesh PWs to the primary PE (PE1-rs). After the MTU-s switches to the backup spoke PW, traffic toward those addresses is black-holed until the MAC aging timer expires (the default is 5 minutes) or a packet from the address arrives via the new PE (PE2-rs).

Under RFC 4762, a PE that receives a MAC flush message removes all MAC addresses for that VPLS instance except those learned over the PW the message arrived on. The RFC calls this positive flushing, or "flush-all-but-mine". Addresses that did not change are flushed too, so unknown-destination flooding and relearning happen throughout the network. The cost grows with the number of PEs in the mesh and the number of VPLS instances. Only the addresses learned over the PWs to PE1-rs need to go.

PBB-VPLS has a similar problem. Remote PEs learn a customer MAC (C-MAC) against the backbone MAC (B-MAC) of the PE that was active. When the customer link fails over, they keep sending to the old B-MAC. Flushing that B-MAC with RFC 4762 would cause much unnecessary flushing in the backbone, where nothing changed. The native Ethernet access case, such as ITU-T G.8032 rings or multi-chassis LAG emulations, has the same issue.
sections.eli5: Today, when one road closes, every switch throws away all its directions except one. That wastes time, because most directions were fine.

sections.title: Negative MAC Flushing
sections.content:
The fix is negative MAC flushing, or "flush-all-from-me". When PE1-rs detects failure of its primary spoke PW (or a change from active to standby), it sends a MAC flush message to the PEs in the full mesh. Each receiver identifies the VPLS instance and the PW terminating at PE1-rs from the FEC TLV and/or LDP session, and flushes only the addresses learned over that PW.

PE1-rs should initiate this only if it is dual-homing aware, meaning some redundancy mechanism runs between the MTU-s and its PEs. If it is agnostic, it should not flush on failure, since that could cause needless flushing for a single-homed MTU-s. When the MTU-s itself triggers the flush on switching to the backup PW, the method is modeled on the Topology Change Notification of the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol: the receiver flushes everything except what it learned over that link, then relays the message onward.

Messages follow the data-plane split-horizon rules of H-VPLS: a flush received on a spoke PW is propagated to mesh PWs, but one received on a mesh PW is not propagated to other mesh PWs. If a negative flush carries a MAC list, it SHOULD contain only the MACs of the affected MTU-s. If the list is empty, all MTU-s devices attached to the originating PE are flushed and relearned.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone forgetting everything except one thing, the switch that lost a road says: forget only the directions that went through me.

sections.title: The MAC Flush Parameters TLV
sections.content:
RFC 7361 defines a new LDP TLV, the MAC Flush Parameters TLV (also called the MAC Flush TLV), with type 0x0406. The U-bit and F-bit are both set so that intermediate VPLS PEs unaware of the TLV forward it transparently. It SHOULD be placed after the existing TLVs in the RFC 4762 MAC flush message. The value holds a mandatory 1-byte Flags field and MAY carry one or more sub-TLVs.

Two flags are defined. The C flag gives the PBB-VPLS context: 0 for the backbone VPLS (B-VPLS), 1 for the customer I-component. In regular H-VPLS it MUST be 0. The N flag selects positive (0, flush-all-but-mine) or negative (1, flush-all-from-me) action; for the optimized procedure it MUST be 1. The remaining bits are MBZ (must be zero) and are ignored on reception.

If a message carries this TLV with N = 0 or N = 1 and also a valid MAC address list, receivers SHOULD ignore the option and handle the MACs explicitly as in RFC 4762.
sections.eli5: The message gets a small extra note with two switches. One says which part of the network this is about, and the other says whether to forget everything but me or only things from me.

sections.title: Processing Rules for VPLS and PBB-VPLS
sections.content:
In regular VPLS, a multi-homing PE-rs that detects a transition in its active spoke PW sends the TLV with N = 1 inside an address withdraw message with an empty MAC list. A receiver with N = 1 SHOULD flush all MAC addresses learned from the PW on which the message arrived. With N = 0 it SHOULD flush the addresses from all PWs in the instance except that one. With Multi-Segment PWs, only the terminating PEs act, and switching PEs pass the message along. With provider RSTP selecting the active PW (as in the document's Figure 4), PE1-rs MAY trigger the flush when it sees its PW fail.

For PBB-VPLS, two sub-TLVs are defined, and at least one MUST appear when C = 1. The PBB B-MAC List Sub-TLV (type 0x0407) carries one or more 48-bit B-MACs of the originator. The PBB I-SID List Sub-TLV (type 0x0408) carries 24-bit I-SIDs, and an empty list means all I-SIDs mapped to the B-VPLS.

Backbone Core Bridges, when C = 1, SHOULD NOT flush their B-MAC FIBs and SHOULD propagate the message following split-horizon rules. Backbone Edge Bridges use the I-SID list to pick which I-component FIBs to consider (all if absent) and the B-MAC list to pick which B-MAC-to-C-MAC associations (all if absent). With N = 0 they SHOULD flush all C-MACs in the selected FIBs except those tied to the listed B-MACs. With N = 1 they SHOULD flush the C-MACs tied to the listed B-MACs.
sections.eli5: In a bigger network with many labeled sections, the note can also list which sections and which senders to forget, so each switch erases only those.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
A receiver that does not understand the TLV may take an undesirable flushing action. The RFC says all devices should understand the TLV before it is turned on, and RECOMMENDS that all PE-rs devices in PBB-VPLS support it; where that is not possible, it SHOULD be disabled. It discusses an LDP capability negotiation mechanism but considers it out of scope and states that negotiation is not required to deploy the optimization.

Operators are responsible for configuring capable devices correctly, and implementations are RECOMMENDED to offer administrative control over which flushing action is used toward each PE-rs. During upgrades, one PE could send optimized messages to capable peers while another sends RFC 4762 style messages to peers that lack support. A PE-rs that supports the new TLV MUST still support the RFC 4762 procedures, since this document only augments them.
sections.eli5: If some switches do not understand the new note, they might erase too much, so an operator should switch it on only where every switch can read it.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA allocated three LDP TLV type values: 0x0406 (MAC Flush Parameters TLV), 0x0407 (PBB B-MAC List Sub-TLV) and 0x0408 (PBB I-SID List Sub-TLV). It also created a sub-registry called MAC Flush Flags, with bit 0 (0x80) as C and bit 1 (0x40) as N, bits 2 to 7 unassigned, and new bits assigned by Standards Action.

For security, LDP authentication methods from RFC 5036 apply, and the document follows the considerations in RFC 4447 and RFC 4762. The RFC argues that optimizing flushing reduces the risk of attacks, but if the configuration of support for the new TLV can be spoofed, sub-optimal behavior will result. It states there is no impact on the VPLS forwarding plane.
sections.eli5: The new note gets its own official number, and the usual protections for these messages still apply. If someone fakes the setting, the network just works less efficiently.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: C and N flags followed by must-be-zero bits.

cells: All MACs in the instance except those learned over the PW the message arrived on (flush-all-but-mine)
Only MACs learned from the sender's PW (flush-all-from-me)

items.label: MAC Flush Parameters TLV
items.desc: Carries the Flags byte and optional sub-TLVs.

items.label: PBB B-MAC List Sub-TLV
items.desc: One or more 48-bit B-MAC addresses of the originator.

items.label: PBB I-SID List Sub-TLV
items.desc: One or more 24-bit I-SIDs; empty means all.
